clue.text: Pair of hacks look smart

indicators.note: a pair means two of something, so the word for a hack is written twice over

parts.note: to hack at something is to chop it, so hacks are chops

explanation.surface: Two journalists try to look well turned out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hacks' reads as journalists but here means cutting strokes. 'Look smart' is the British idiom for hurry up.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are informal commands urging someone to hurry, so the idiom and the reduplicated exclamation are synonyms.

clue.text: Doctor's boring journeys over this ultimately do drag

indicators.note: something boring drills into another thing, so the doctor goes inside the other piece

parts.note: to journey over a river or road is to cross it, so journeys over means crosses
DR is the usual abbreviation for doctor; the 's is just a link

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the final letter of this is used

explanation.surface: A tedious physician's travels end with a drag act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like dull but signals that DR drills into CROSSES; then the S ending 'this' is added.
explanation.definitionFit: To do drag is to perform in clothes of the opposite sex, which is exactly the meaning of the hyphenated verb.

clue.text: Tolkien character ranks third amongst suchlike

parts.note: OR stands for Other Ranks, soldiers who are not officers

indicators.note: third amongst asks for the letter in third position within the word suchlike

explanation.surface: A Middle-earth figure comes third in a list of similar creatures.
explanation.walkthrough: OR (Other Ranks, ordinary soldiers) is a crossword staple for 'ranks'; the third letter of 'suchlike' is C.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolkien's fantasy novels populate Middle-earth with brutish goblin soldiers of this kind, so one is an example of his characters.

clue.text: Gas enshrouding battleground a symbol of death

indicators.note: a shroud wraps a body, so the gas letters wrap around the battleground

parts.note: CS gas is the tear gas used in riot control
Ypres in Belgium was the scene of three great battles of the First World War

explanation.surface: Poison gas drifting over a war-torn field becomes an image of mortality.
explanation.walkthrough: Ypres is the Flanders town fought over in the First World War; CS is the tear gas.
explanation.definitionFit: This dark evergreen is traditionally planted in graveyards and has long been an emblem of mourning and mortality.

clue.text: Ease excessively limp characters into circle to make poetry

indicators.note: into tells us one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: a circle has the shape of the letter O
to versify is to write verse, to make poetry

indicators.note: characters here means the letters of limp, taken as a set to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Putting weak letters inside a ring to compose verse makes things too easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' signals that the letters of 'limp' are shuffled to MPLI, which goes 'into' O plus VERSIFY.
explanation.definitionFit: To ease something is to simplify it, so easing it excessively is going too far in simplification.

clue.text: Stars not demanding bright clothing

indicators.note: clothing means dressing around, so one word wraps the other

parts.note: gay in its older sense means bright and colourful
lax means relaxed or not strict, so not demanding

explanation.surface: Celebrities who are easygoing dress in vivid outfits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' tempts as celebrities, but it is the definition in its astronomical sense; GAY is used in its old meaning of bright.
explanation.definitionFit: A galaxy is a vast system of stars bound together by gravity, so stars collectively make one up.

clue.text: Business taking off in area of recession in East End?

indicators.note: the Cockney speech of London's East End famously drops the initial H from words

parts.note: a receding hairline is where hair retreats from the forehead

explanation.surface: A firm flourishing in a depressed part of east London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recession' suggests the economy but means a receding hairline; Cockneys of London's East End drop their H's, so HAIRLINE loses its H.
explanation.definitionFit: A carrier flying passengers is literally a business whose planes take off, so the phrase is a witty description.

clue.text: Swift work finding a relation from Bath?

parts.note: a relation is a telling or account, that is a tale
of can mean from, as in coming of good stock
a bath is a tub, so with an article it becomes a tub

explanation.surface: Discovering a relative who comes from the English spa city of Bath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bath' looks like the English spa city but just means a tub; 'relation' is an account, not a relative. Jonathan Swift wrote this satire in 1704.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonathan Swift's satire on religious divisions bears this title, so it is a work by him.

clue.text: Pull one across pond

definitions.meaning: to give a sharp tug or jerk
an American, someone from across the Atlantic, in British slang

explanation.definitionFit: A sharp tug is a yank, and British slang calls any American a Yank, the pond being the Atlantic.

clue.text: Employed old copper bearing clubs as rat-catcher

indicators.note: bearing means carrying, so the old copper carries the clubs inside it

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
the Pied Piper of Hamelin was the legendary rat-catcher

explanation.surface: An elderly policeman carrying a truncheon has taken a job catching rats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old copper' suggests a retired policeman but is O plus Cu, the chemical symbol, holding C; the Pied Piper is the rat-catcher of the legend.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone employed has their time taken up by work, which is the sense of being busy or engaged.

clue.text: Lay down and died in drought?

indicators.note: in signals that one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a drought is zero rain, written as O for nothing followed by rain
D is the usual abbreviation for died, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: Someone collapsed and perished in a time of dry weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay down' looks like a past tense, but it is the verb 'to lay down', meaning to decree. A drought is 'nought rain': O plus RAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay down a rule is to decree it formally, the same as to ordain it.

clue.text: Saved article made of iron coming in contact with acid

parts.note: to iron clothes is to press them
an acid remark is biting or cutting

explanation.surface: A piece of metal touches a corrosive chemical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron' and 'acid' read as chemistry but mean PRESS (as in ironing) and CUTTING (as in a sharp remark).
explanation.definitionFit: An item clipped from a newspaper and kept is a newspaper clipping, so it is a saved article.

clue.text: Superior waiting as sister failing to pen one-line poem

indicators.note: to pen something is to enclose it, so sister surrounds the poem

parts.note: SR is the abbreviation for sister, as for a nun or nurse
I is the Roman numeral one
a verse is a short poem
a failing is a fault or vice

explanation.surface: A nun is failing to write a single line of poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waiting' is table service, not delay. The stray 'ok' is an OCR artefact the wordplay does not use.
explanation.definitionFit: Silver service is the formal style of serving food at table, so it is high-class waiting by waiting staff.

clue.text: Don't go ringing up one rich female for help

indicators.note: ringing means encircling, so the first piece surrounds the others

parts.note: to linger is to stay on rather than leave

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the letters are read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
rich food is fat

explanation.surface: A plea not to leave as someone telephones a wealthy woman for assistance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringing up' suggests a telephone call, but 'up' turns the three pieces round in this down clue, giving FTAFI, and 'ringing' means the stay-on word surrounds them.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom to lift a finger means to make the slightest effort to help, usually used in the negative.

clue.text: Scotsman cracking gag in Wales

indicators.note: cracking means breaking up, so these letters are broken and rearranged

explanation.surface: A man from Scotland telling a joke while in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracking' looks like telling a joke but signals the anagram of GAG IN WALES.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Glasgow, Scotland's largest city, is a particular kind of Scot.

clue.text: Chap making our demand for riot cover heard

indicators.note: heard signals that the letters are taken from how the words sound spoken

parts.note: a plea for shelter during a riot would be a call to roof us over

explanation.surface: A man joins the protesters' cry for shelter from the trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The plea 'roof us!' asking for cover, said out loud, gives the man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Rufus is a man's given name, and crosswords use any male name as a chap.

clue.text: Expert worries about being eaten by savage

indicators.note: being eaten by puts the first piece inside the savage piece

parts.note: to savage is to maul, as an animal does

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: worries as a verb means frets

explanation.surface: A specialist's anxieties are consumed by a wild animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expert' is an adjective here; 'about' turns the worries word round to give STERF, and 'being eaten by' puts it inside the savage word.
explanation.definitionFit: Masterful means showing great skill, which is what an expert performance shows.

clue.text: Boils ham for carving cold in mess

indicators.note: carving cuts things up, so the letters are cut and rearranged

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A cook boils ham for carving while the kitchen is chaotic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carving' signals an anagram of BOILS HAM, then C for cold.
explanation.definitionFit: Shambolic is British slang for chaotic or disorganised, which is the state of being in a mess.

clue.text: President in position to look for reds here?

parts.note: the Cold War scare about reds under the bed suggests looking under one
Gerald Ford was the 38th US President

explanation.surface: A Cold War president is poised to hunt for communists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reds under the bed' was a Cold War scare about hidden communists. Bedford is an English county town, and 'here?' makes the whole clue describe it.
explanation.definitionFit: The question mark makes the clue describe a town, which is where the words point, so it names a place cryptically.

clue.text: Spirit connected with ghost regoes er regularly

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held reads 'Spirit connected with ghost regoes er regularly': 'regoes er' is garbled OCR; the blog parses MET + alternate letters of ghost, but the true wording is not recoverable.
annotationWithheld.clue: Spirit connected with ghost regoes er regularly

clue.text: Assailants mount stick up on one side of Scottish city

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the letters are read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: gum is glue, something that sticks
the Gers is the nickname of Rangers, one of Glasgow's two big football teams

explanation.surface: Attackers climb up and plant a stick on one side of a Scottish city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' reverses GUM. Glasgow Rangers, one of the city's two big football clubs, are known as the Gers.
explanation.definitionFit: Muggers attack people in the street to rob them, so they are assailants.

clue.text: Persistent beating failed to reform

indicators.note: to reform is to be formed again, so the letters take a new order

explanation.surface: A beating that failed to make someone change their ways, which keeps on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To reform' signals an anagram of BEATING FAILED. The stray 'on,' is an OCR artefact.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who never tires keeps going, which is what being persistent means.

clue.text: Passing information round section

parts.note: a round shape is the letter O
a section is a bit or part

explanation.surface: Information is passed around to a department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passing' looks like handing over, but it means dying: the definition is a death notice.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for obituary, a notice giving news of someone's death, that is of their passing.

clue.text: Most significant digit in base five

definitions.text: Most significant digit in base five

parts.words: Most significant digit in base five
parts.note: sounds like number theory, but means the largest of the five toes at the base of the leg, the foot

explanation.definitionFit: The largest toe is the biggest of five digits on the foot, the body's base.

clue.text: Low-calorie peach: one they devour a lot

parts.note: lite is the commercial spelling for low-calorie products
to peach is old slang for informing on someone, to rat
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A diet peach is one fruit that people eat plenty of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peach' is the old verb meaning to inform, so RAT. The definition is about devouring books.
explanation.definitionFit: Literary people read voraciously, so they devour a lot of books, a playful description of them.

clue.text: Wings of annoyed duck flapping

indicators.note: the wings of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: a duck is a score of nought in cricket, written O

explanation.surface: An irritated duck beats its wings.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a duck is a score of zero, hence O; 'flapping' is the noun 'a flap', a fuss.
explanation.definitionFit: A flapping is informal for a state of agitation or fuss, as is ado.

clue.text: Diatribe on reflection played a ritual part

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror is reversed, so the letters read backwards
part means only some letters of the words are used

explanation.surface: A ranting speech that, looked back on, acted a ceremonial role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' signals letters hidden in 'played a ritual'; 'on reflection' reads EDARIT backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A diatribe is a bitter, angry speech of denunciation, the same as a long rant.

clue.text: Encourages Pat's employer to provide cracking little scoop

indicators.note: cracking means breaking into, so the employer breaks into the encouraging words

parts.note: to egg on is to urge or encourage
Postman Pat, the British children's TV postman, works for the Post Office, PO

explanation.surface: Urging the postman's boss to supply something small for news.
explanation.walkthrough: Postman Pat is a British children's TV postman, so his employer is the PO (Post Office). 'Cracking' puts PO into EGGS ON.
explanation.definitionFit: This small utensil is used for eating boiled eggs, so it is a little scoop.
